hook.support: You're good at something: fixing bikes, baking, mowing, braiding hair. People would pay for it. How much? How will they find out?
hook.core: You're good at something. Braiding hair. Fixing bikes. Baking. Mowing. Editing videos. Explaining maths so it actually makes sense. People would pay for it. But how much do you charge? How will anyone find out? And when does a bit of cash on the side become a real business?

why.support: Lots of teens want their own business. To start, you need to **price** it, **pitch** it and **promote** it. Those are all reading, writing and speaking jobs.
why.core: Lots of teenagers want to run their own business one day. What stops most of them isn't ideas. It's knowing how to **price** it, **pitch** it and **promote** it. Every one of those is a literacy job: a spoken pitch that hooks people, a flyer that persuades honestly, and the reading you need to know your responsibilities.
why.extend: Turning a skill into income requires persuasive texts across modes (a structured spoken pitch and a multimodal flyer) designed for a specific customer, plus the careful reading needed to understand pricing, consumer responsibilities and when an activity becomes a business.

articles.title: Turn a skill into cash

body.support:
A **side hustle** is a small way to earn money.

**1. Find your offer.** Your skill + someone who needs it. *I'll fix bikes for families on my street.*

**2. Check it's OK.** Talk to a parent or carer. Work with people you know.

**3. Price it.** Add your **costs**, like parts. Add your time. Check what others charge.

**4. Pitch it.** In 30 seconds, say:

- the **problem**: *Flat tyre?*
- your **offer**: *I'll fix it.*
- **why you**: *I've done it for years.*
- the **price**
- what to do: *Text to book.*

**5. Promote it.** Make a flyer: a headline, a picture, the price, how to book. Be honest. Under 16? Use noticeboards and word of mouth.

**6. Hobby or business?** Just for fun, now and then? It's a hobby. Regular, for profit? It might be a business.
body.core:
A **side hustle** is a small way to earn money on your own terms. Here's how to start one.

**1. Find your offer.** An offer is a skill plus someone who needs it. *I can fix bikes* becomes *I'll fix bikes for families on my street, at their place, on weekends.* Think about who your **customer** is, and what problem you solve for them.

**2. Check it's safe and OK.** Talk to a parent or carer. Work with people you or your family know. Some things, like selling food to the public, may need permission from your local council, so check first.

**3. Price it.** Add up your **costs**: materials, tools, transport. Add something for your time. Then check what others charge, so your price is fair. What's left after costs is your **profit**.

**4. Pitch it.** A **pitch** is a short spoken text that persuades. A strong 30-second pitch has:

- the **problem**: *Flat tyre? Bike sitting in the shed?*
- your **offer**: *I fix bikes at your place, this weekend.*
- **why you**: *I've fixed my whole family's bikes for three years.*
- the **price**
- a **call to action**: *Ask your parents to text mine to book.*

Speak slowly, look at your audience, and finish strong.

**5. Promote it.** A flyer or poster needs a headline that names the problem, a clear picture, the price, and how to book. Be honest: Australian Consumer Law means businesses can't mislead customers. No fake reviews, and no promises you can't keep. If you're under 16, you can't hold accounts on platforms like TikTok and Instagram. Use school or community noticeboards, word of mouth and your family's help instead.

**6. Hobby or business?** If you do it now and then, for fun, it's probably a **hobby**. If you do it regularly, to make a profit, it may be a **business**. Businesses can get an **ABN**, and may need to pay tax. business.gov.au has a free guide to tell the difference.
body.extend:
A **side hustle** converts a skill into income. Each stage depends on a different kind of text.

**1. Define the offer:** a skill matched to a specific **customer** and problem. *I can fix bikes* becomes *weekend, at-home bike repairs for families on my street.*

**2. Check suitability and safety.** Involve a parent or carer, start with known customers, and check regulatory requirements. Some activities, such as selling food to the public, may need council approval.

**3. Set a price** that covers **costs** (materials, tools, transport) and values your time, informed by what competitors charge. **Profit** is what remains after costs.

**4. Structure the pitch.** A persuasive 30-second spoken text moves from **problem** to **offer**, **credibility** (*why you*), **price** and a **call to action**. Delivery (pace, eye contact and a strong close) matters as much as content.

**5. Promote responsibly.** A flyer's headline, image, price and booking details work together to persuade. Australian Consumer Law prohibits misleading claims, so testimonials must be real and promises deliverable. Under-16s can't hold accounts on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, so offline channels (noticeboards, word of mouth, family networks) matter.

**6. Distinguish hobby from business.** Occasional activity for enjoyment is generally a **hobby**. Regular activity with a profit motive may be a **business**, which can register for an **ABN** and may have tax obligations. business.gov.au explains the difference.

caseStudies.title: Half of students want to be their own boss

body.support:
**NAB** is a big bank. In **2025**, it asked secondary students about their plans.

What it found:

- **47%** want to start their **own business**.
- In **2023**, it was **35%**.
- The biggest problem: they don't have **practical experience**.

So lots of students want a business. But they need to learn how. That's what this course is for.
body.core:
**NAB**, one of Australia's big banks, surveys secondary school students about their plans. In **2025**, it shared its latest results.

Here's what it found:

- **47%** of secondary students said they want to start their **own business** after school.
- That's up from **35%** in **2023**.
- More boys (**52%**) than girls (**41%**) said they wanted to.
- The main things holding students back were **limited resources** and a **lack of practical experience**.

So wanting to start a business is common. What's missing for many students is knowing **how**: how to price something, how to pitch it, and how to get customers.

That's exactly what you'll practise in this course. A side hustle now, even a small one, is practical experience you can't get from reading about business.
body.extend:
**NAB**, one of Australia's big banks, surveys secondary students about their plans after school. Its **2025** results showed:

- **47%** of secondary students want to start their **own business** after school, up from **35%** in **2023**.
- More boys (**52%**) than girls (**41%**) said so.
- Students named **limited resources** and a **lack of practical experience** as the main barriers.

The most interesting finding is the gap between wanting and knowing how. Lots of students have the ambition. Far fewer have the practical skills: pricing, pitching and promoting.

A small side hustle builds those skills early. And each one depends on persuasive texts written for real customers.

teacher.overview: A Crossroads capstone combining Money Moves and Digital Life. Students plan a small side hustle: defining an offer for a specific customer, pricing it from costs, time and competitors, writing and delivering a structured 30-second spoken pitch, and designing an honest multimodal flyer. They read about responsibilities: safety, misleading claims under consumer law, the difference between a hobby and a business, and safe promotion for under-16s. The case study is NAB's 2025 survey of secondary students' business aspirations.
prep: Organise a pitch panel: staff, older students, or local business people (a council youth officer or a local trader works well).
Have A4 paper and coloured pens, or a simple design app, for the flyers.
Decide whether any side hustles will actually run (e.g. a school market day), and check school policies.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** problem, offer, why you, price, call to action. Price: add costs, add your time, check what others charge. Hobby: occasional, for fun, around cost; business: regular, with a profit motive, may need an ABN and pay tax.

**Sort:** knitted scarves at cost — hobby; six lawns weekly — business; birthday cake — hobby; regular video clients — business; weekly sneaker reselling — business; selling old clothes — hobby.

**Flyer:** 1 headline (names the problem); 2 image (shows the result); 3 offer (what, where, when); 4 credibility; 5 clear prices; 6 safe call to action through a parent.

**Case study:** 47% of secondary students want to start a business, up from 35% in 2023; more boys (52%) than girls (41%); barriers were limited resources and lack of practical experience; a side hustle builds that experience.

realityCheck: **Safety first.** Students should only offer services to people they or their families know, and book through a parent or carer.
**Not every idea is allowed.** Selling food, offering childcare or anything involving tools and strangers may need adult supervision or council rules. Help students choose sensible ideas.
**Money can be sensitive.** Some students need to earn; others don't. Keep the focus on skills.
**Tax and ABNs.** Keep it simple: point students to business.gov.au and the ATO, and don't give individual tax advice.
**Works in a real class:** yes. The pitch panel is a highlight, especially with real local business people.
